# Single-frequency lasers: DBR, DFB, external cavity, VCSEL {#sec-single-mode} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/single-mode.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slides 140–144 (distributed Bragg reflector and distributed feedback lasers, commercial devices, example on the DFB wavelength), 145–146 (external cavity laser diodes) and 147–151 (vertical cavity surface emitting lasers).* ## Key relations A Fabry–Perot laser diode oscillates on several modes, and hops between them (@sec-ld-structures). WDM systems (Ch. 2) need one wavelength, stable to a fraction of 0.8 nm. The solution is a mirror whose reflectance depends on wavelength: a **Bragg grating** (Ch. 1, Bragg mirrors; Ch. 2, fiber Bragg gratings). A corrugation of period $\Lambda$ reflects strongly only near the Bragg wavelength (slide 140b) $$ \lambda_B=\frac{2n\Lambda}{q},\qquad q=1,2,\dots\ \text{(order)}. $$ * In a **DBR laser** (slide 140) the gratings replace the facets, outside the pumped region. * In a **DFB laser** (slides 141–142) the grating runs along the whole active region: feedback is distributed. A uniform grating does not lase *at* $\lambda_B$ but on two modes just outside the stop band (slide 142), $$\lambda_m=\lambda_B\pm\frac{\lambda_B^2}{2nL}(m+1).$$ An asymmetry (a facet coating, or a quarter-wave phase shift in the middle of the grating) selects one of them. * An **external cavity laser** (slides 145–146) uses an AR-coated diode chip, a lens and an external grating or filter: long cavity, narrow linewidth (kHz), tunable. * A **VCSEL** (slides 147–151) has a cavity about one wavelength long between two epitaxial DBR mirrors. The mode spacing is so large that only one longitudinal mode fits under the gain curve, but the single-pass gain is tiny, so the mirrors need $R>99$ %. ## Worked example: DFB wavelength (slide 144), recomputed > DFB laser with corrugation period $\Lambda=0.22$ µm, grating length 400 µm, effective index 3.5, first order. Find the Bragg > wavelength, the mode wavelengths and their separation. ::: {#tbl-dfb .cell tbl-cap='Slide 144 recomputed with Kasap\'s formula λ_m = λ_B ± λ_B²(m + 1)/(2nL), m = 0.' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} lB, lm, lp = lz.dfb_modes(0.22e-6, 3.5, 400e-6, m=[0]) pd.DataFrame([("Bragg wavelength λ_B = 2nΛ", f"{lB*1e6:.4f} µm"), ("mode below λ_B (m = 0)", f"{lm[0]*1e6:.5f} µm"), ("mode above λ_B (m = 0)", f"{lp[0]*1e6:.5f} µm"), ("separation of the two modes", f"{(lp - lm)[0]*1e9:.2f} nm")], columns=["quantity", "value"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Coupled-mode theory of a grating (going further on slides 140–142) The slide formula treats the grating as a pair of mirrors. Coupled-mode theory (forward and backward waves coupled by the grating with coefficient $\kappa=\pi\Delta n/\lambda$) gives the exact response of a uniform grating of length $L$, with or without gain. Passive, it is the fiber Bragg grating of Ch. 2: a stop band of width $\Delta\lambda\approx\lambda_B^2\kappa/(\pi n)$ for strong gratings, with peak reflectance $\tanh^2(\kappa L)$. With gain, the transmission diverges at the frequencies where the structure can oscillate by itself: the DFB laser modes. ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {gratingRT, cabs2, dbrSpectrum} from "./laser_sim.js" viewof gr = Inputs.form({ kL: Inputs.range([0.2, 5], {value: 2, step: 0.05, label: "coupling strength κL"}), gL: Inputs.range([0, 4], {value: 0, step: 0.01, label: "net gain gL (power gain × length)"}), shift: Inputs.radio(["uniform grating", "λ/4 phase shift in the middle"], {value: "uniform grating", label: "grating"}), view: Inputs.radio(["reflectance |r|²", "transmission |t|² (log)"], {value: "reflectance |r|²", label: "plot"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false grOut = { const L = 400e-6, neff = 3.5, Lam = 0.22e-6, lB = 2*neff*Lam, dn = gr.kL*lB/(Math.PI*L), g = gr.gL/L, data = []; let best = {T: 0}; for (let i = 0; i <= 1200; i++) { const wl = lB - 4e-9 + 8e-9*i/1200, {r, t} = gratingRT(wl, Lam, neff, dn, L, g, gr.shift.startsWith("λ") ? Math.PI/2 : 0); const d = {wl: wl*1e9, R: cabs2(r), T: cabs2(t)}; data.push(d); if (d.T > best.T) best = d; } return {data, lB, best, dlB: lB*lB/(2*neff*L)}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 290, x: {label: "wavelength (nm)"}, y: gr.view.startsWith("refl") ? {label: "|r|²", grid: true} : {label: "|t|²", type: "log", grid: true}, marks: [Plot.line(grOut.data, {x: "wl", y: gr.view.startsWith("refl") ? "R" : "T", stroke: "#4a3aa7", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleX([grOut.lB*1e9], {stroke: "#52514e", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}), Plot.ruleX([grOut.lB*1e9 - grOut.dlB*1e9, grOut.lB*1e9 + grOut.dlB*1e9], {stroke: "#eb6834", strokeDasharray: "2,4"})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
λB = ${(grOut.lB*1e9).toFixed(2)} nm (grey) · Kasap's modes λB ± λB²/2nL (orange) · peak reflectance ${d3.max(grOut.data, d => d.R).toFixed(4)} (passive tanh²κL = ${(Math.tanh(gr.kL)**2).toFixed(4)}) · largest transmission ${grOut.best.T.toExponential(2)} at ${grOut.best.wl.toFixed(3)} nm
` ``` Things to try: * With $gL=0$, increase $\kappa L$: the stop band widens and the reflectance approaches 1. * Raise the gain with the uniform grating and the transmission plot: two peaks grow symmetrically **on each side** of the stop band. At the gain where they diverge, the laser oscillates on both: the two-mode problem of slide 142. * Switch to the λ/4-shifted grating: a single peak grows **at** $\lambda_B$, in the middle of the stop band, and it diverges at a lower gain. All modern telecom DFB lasers use a λ/4 shift or an asymmetric facet coating. ::: {#cell-fig-dfb-threshold .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} wl = np.linspace(1.536e-6, 1.544e-6, 6001) dn = 2*1.54e-6/(np.pi*400e-6) gs = np.linspace(0, 12000, 120) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.6)) for sh, lab in ((0, "uniform"), (np.pi/2, "λ/4 shifted")): Tm = [np.max(np.abs(lz.grating_rt(wl, 0.22e-6, 3.5, dn, 400e-6, g=g, shift=sh)[1])**2) for g in gs] ax.semilogy(gs*400e-6, Tm, label=lab) ax.set(xlabel="gL", ylabel="max |t|²", ylim=(0.5, 1e6)); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Peak transmission of an amplifying grating (κL = 2, L = 400 µm) versus gain. The first divergence marks the lasing threshold: gL ≈ 1.4 for the λ/4-shifted grating, on a single mode at λ_B, against gL ≈ 2.0 for the uniform grating, whose two edge modes reach threshold together. The later peaks are higher-order modes.](single-mode_files/figure-html/fig-dfb-threshold-output-1.png){#fig-dfb-threshold width=697 height=381} ::: ::: ## Linewidths in the commercial tables (slide 143) Spectral widths are quoted in frequency or wavelength, $\delta\lambda=\lambda^2\delta\nu/c$: ::: {#tbl-linewidth .cell tbl-cap='Slide 143: conversion between δν and δλ. The table footnote should read \'fm is 10⁻¹⁵ m\' (not s).' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} items = [("DBR, 1063 nm", 1063e-9, 2e6, "8 fm"), ("DFB, 1063 nm", 1063e-9, 2e6, "8 fm"), ("DFB, 1550 nm", 1550e-9, 10e6, "0.08 pm"), ("EC laser, 1550 nm", 1550e-9, 50e3, "0.4 fm"), ("FP laser (slide 100), 1550 nm", 1550e-9, None, "1.3 nm")] rows = [] for name, lam, dnu, ref in items: if dnu is None: rows.append({"laser": name, "δν": f"{lz.c0*1.3e-9/lam**2/1e9:.0f} GHz", "δλ": "1.3 nm", "slide": ref, "coherence length c/πδν": f"{lz.c0/(np.pi*lz.c0*1.3e-9/lam**2)*1e3:.2f} mm"}) else: rows.append({"laser": name, "δν": f"{dnu/1e6:g} MHz", "δλ": f"{lam**2*dnu/lz.c0*1e15:.2f} fm", "slide": ref, "coherence length c/πδν": f"{lz.c0/(np.pi*dnu):.3g} m"}) pd.DataFrame(rows) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: A single-frequency laser is more coherent than a Fabry–Perot laser by six orders of magnitude (Ch. 1, coherence length). The remaining linewidth comes from spontaneous emission into the lasing mode: see [Going further: laser linewidth](linewidth-noise.qmd). ## VCSEL mirrors (slides 147–151) In a VCSEL the light crosses a gain region only a few quantum wells thick, about 30 nm. The single-pass gain is about $e^{gd}\approx1.003$ for $g=1000$ cm⁻¹, so the mirrors must lose less than 0.3 % per pass. Epitaxial AlAs/GaAs quarter-wave stacks (Ch. 1, Bragg mirrors) provide this: ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof vc = Inputs.form({ N: Inputs.range([5, 40], {value: 25, step: 1, label: "number of DBR pairs N"}), nH: Inputs.range([3.0, 3.7], {value: 3.52, step: 0.01, label: "high index (GaAs)"}), nL: Inputs.range([1.5, 3.4], {value: 2.95, step: 0.01, label: "low index (AlAs; ≈ 1.6 for oxidised AlOx)"}), dact: Inputs.range([5, 100], {value: 24, step: 1, label: "total QW thickness (nm)"}), Gr: Inputs.range([1.0, 2.0], {value: 1.8, step: 0.05, label: "longitudinal enhancement (standing wave)"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false vcOut = { const wl0 = 850e-9, spec = []; for (let i = 0; i <= 400; i++) { const wl = 700e-9 + 300e-9*i/400; spec.push({wl: wl*1e9, R: dbrSpectrum(wl, vc.N, vc.nH, vc.nL, 1.0, vc.nH, wl0)}); } const R = dbrSpectrum(wl0, vc.N, vc.nH, vc.nL, vc.nH, vc.nH, wl0); // mirror seen from inside the cavity const d = vc.dact*1e-9, gth = Math.log(1/(R*R))/(2*d*vc.Gr)/100; // cm^-1 (internal loss neglected) return {spec, R, gth}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 250, x: {label: "wavelength (nm)"}, y: {label: "DBR reflectance (from air)", domain: [0, 1], grid: true}, marks: [Plot.line(vcOut.spec, {x: "wl", y: "R", stroke: "#2a78d6", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleX([850], {stroke: "#52514e", strokeDasharray: "3,3"})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
reflectance at 850 nm, seen from the cavity: ${(100*vcOut.R).toFixed(4)} % · threshold gain with two such mirrors: ${vcOut.gth.toFixed(0)} cm⁻¹ ${vcOut.gth < 3000 ? "(reachable with strained QWs)" : "(too high: add pairs)"}
` ``` ::: {#tbl-vcsel .cell tbl-cap='Slide 149 with recomputed slope efficiency and wavelength–frequency conversion of the linewidth.' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} v = pd.DataFrame([(680, "<0.1", 0.046, 21, 0.4, 3, 2.8, 0.95, 0.32, "STM"), (680, "0.5", 0.04, 15, 2.5, 8, 2.3, 4, 0.7, "MTM"), (850, "0.0002", 0.06, 17, 0.5, 2, 2.2, 0.75, 0.5, "STM"), (850, "<0.65", 0.06, 26, 1, 6, 1.9, 2, 0.4, "MTM")], columns=["λ (nm)", "δλ (nm)", "dλ/dT (nm/K)", "Δθ (°)", "I_th (mA)", "I (mA)", "V (V)", "P_o (mW)", "slope, slide", "type"]) v["slope = P_o/(I − I_th)"] = (v["P_o (mW)"]/(v["I (mA)"] - v["I_th (mA)"])).round(2) v["PCE %"] = (100*v["P_o (mW)"]/(v["I (mA)"]*v["V (V)"])).round(0) v ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The 850 nm single-mode VCSEL has $\delta\lambda=0.2$ pm, that is 83 MHz, and the thresholds are sub-mA: a VCSEL's active volume is a hundred times smaller than an edge emitter's. Low cost (wafer-level testing, 2D arrays, slide 150) made VCSELs the source of short-reach datacom links over multimode fiber (Ch. 2) and of face recognition and lidar modules. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **Hole burning in DFB lasers.** In a λ/4-shifted DFB with large $\kappa L$ the light is concentrated near the phase shift and depletes the carriers there ("longitudinal spatial hole burning"), which can make the laser jump to a side mode at high power. This sets the optimum $\kappa L\approx1$–1.5. - **Tunable lasers.** Sampled-grating DBR lasers combine two combs of reflection peaks with slightly different periods (vernier effect) and tune over 40 nm. Build the two comb spectra numerically and show how a small index change of one comb moves the coincidence by many nm. - **External-cavity linewidth.** The Schawlow–Townes linewidth scales as $1/\tau_{ph}^2$. Lengthening the cavity from 300 µm (chip) to 3 cm (external) multiplies $\tau_{ph}$ by about 100 if the losses per pass are similar: estimate the linewidth reduction. - **VCSEL oxide aperture.** Selective oxidation of an AlGaAs layer creates an AlOx aperture (n ≈ 1.6) that confines both current and light, the key to sub-mA thresholds. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - H. Kogelnik and C. V. Shank, "Coupled-wave theory of distributed feedback lasers", *J. Appl. Phys.* 43, 2327 (1972). - K. Iga, "Surface-emitting laser — its birth and generation of new optoelectronics field", *IEEE J. Sel. Top. Quantum Electron.* 6, 1201 (2000). - Kasap, sec. 4.15–4.17; Coldren *et al.*, ch. 3 (mirrors, gratings) and 8 (tunable lasers). ::: ## Try it yourself 1. A DFB laser must emit at 1550.12 nm (ITU channel 34) with $n_\text{eff}=3.22$. What grating period is needed in first and in second order? 2. With the grating panel, find $\kappa L$ for which the uniform grating reflects 90 %. Compare with $\tanh^2\kappa L$. 3. How many AlAs/GaAs pairs give $R=99.9$ % at 850 nm on a GaAs substrate? And with AlOx/GaAs pairs? 4. Why does a VCSEL need a lower threshold *current* but a higher threshold *gain* than an edge emitter?
